R068-01.notes: C matches P2 (silence frames sounds concertgoers ignore) and the closing 'change in attention ... may be what Cage was after.' A reverses P2 ('Cage insisted that they had not been'); he never admitted a joke. B contradicts the passage's thrust and 'proves' is unsupported. D: the passage claims no 'first ever' and the piano was in fact present (just not played) - unsupported.

R068-02.notes: P1: 'three movements that he marked by opening and closing the lid.' D is the stopwatch trap: he started it, but the passage never says he turned it on and off for each movement. B contradicts 'he played nothing.' C: no announcing is mentioned.

R068-03.notes: P2 lists 'the audience itself, talking and walking out' among the sounds the silence was meant to frame. A assumes the piece is meant to be silent, which Cage denies ('not silent at all'). B: Cage says it was never a joke. C: unsupported; their sounds were part of the piece.

R068-04.notes: P3 opens 'Cage had come to this view partly through an experience' and tells about the anechoic chamber. A is too narrow: the chamber gets only a one-clause definition. C belongs to P2 and is not the job of P3. D: critics come in P4.

R068-05.notes: P3: 'his own nervous system and his own blood in circulation.' D twists the engineer's role: the engineer only explained the sounds. A and B have no support, and the room absorbs sound.

R068-06.notes: Comes straight from the chamber anecdote: even in a soundproof room he heard his own body. B goes against 'does not exist.' C misreads it: the chamber worked, and the remaining sound came from his body. D is about people's preferences, which the passage does not discuss.

flags.note: 'Lasting musical work' paraphrases the second view poorly. The passage says that view sees 'a genuine composition that changes with every performance' and never mentions lasting. 'Lasting' works only as an inferred opposite of the first view's 'idea that loses its force once it has been understood.' Still the only defensible choice, but 'a genuine musical work' would match the text more closely.

R068-07.notes: The two views are 'philosophical statement more than a musical work' versus 'genuine composition.' A, B and C are details the critics never dispute: Tudor performed it, it has three movements, and venue is not discussed.

R068-08.notes: P5: 'Both views, perhaps, miss the piece's quietest achievement ... change in attention.' The stem's 'suggests' fits the hedged 'perhaps.' A: the author never calls it a joke. C: the author says both miss something, not that both are correct. D: neither view is tied to the 1952 performance.

R068-09.notes: The silence frames the ambient sounds, meaning it sets them off so they get noticed. B is the literal-structure trap (a picture frame). C is the other common meaning, 'to frame someone.' D means 'frame a question,' which does not fit sounds.

R068-10.notes: P2: at five minutes the rereaders remembered slightly more, so a five-minute test would wrongly favor rereading. The week-later reversal shows that conclusion is mistaken. B is the true one-week finding, which a five-minute test could not show and which is not a mistake. C is Ebbinghaus's finding from P1 and does not come from a five-minute test. D reverses P3: the rereaders were the more confident ones, and confidence is not what this test measures.
